messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John is a 62-year-old North American male who has been married for over four decades. He works as a potter and finds immense joy in his craft, which he sees as both an art form and a means of expression. John’s life took a tragic turn when his beloved wife, Mary, passed away unexpectedly due to a sudden heart attack. The loss of Mary was devastating for John, and the immediate aftermath was marked by intense grief and shock. As time passed, John began to develop certain patterns that seemed to help him cope with the overwhelming pain he felt. He started pushing away any positive emotions because they made him feel unsafe; these feelings would inevitably lead to a sharp contrast with his current emotional state, making the loss of Mary even more palpable. John also found himself avoiding anything that reminded him of Mary. This included her favorite places, their shared memories, and even simple household items she had used daily. At home, he stopped touching or using these items, as each interaction brought waves of grief and a deep sense of loss. The absence of her presence was overwhelming; every corner seemed to echo with the memory of her laughter or the warmth of her touch. In his occupation, John’s pottery became both an outlet for his pain and another reminder of Mary. He loved making pots because he would often share the pieces they created together at local fairs and art shows. Now, even walking into his studio felt like stepping into a space filled with her absence. The clay on his hands no longer brought joy but rather triggered memories that were too heavy to bear. John also found it increasingly difficult to make plans for the future. The thought of living without Mary made him feel as though any future was meaningless. He stopped setting goals or looking forward to events, both big and small. For instance, he decided not to enter his pottery in competitions anymore; the idea of celebrating success felt hollow and insincere. These maladaptive strategies helped John avoid immediate emotional pain but had long-term consequences on his life and relationships. His avoidance behavior extended beyond personal items and memories; he started pushing away friends and family who tried to comfort him, believing that connecting with others would only lead to more reminders of Mary’s absence. John’s occupational environment also became a source of distress. He closed his studio for weeks at a time when the memories felt too intense. This affected not just his own work but also impacted local sales and community events where he used to showcase his pottery, leading to a decrease in income and a sense of isolation from the broader artistic community. John’s current state is one of profound loneliness and stagnation. He finally decided to seek help after realizing that his coping mechanisms were isolating him further and preventing any form of healing. What frightened him most was not just the pain of losing Mary but the fear that he would never feel whole again, or worse, that he might lose himself in his grief. John is hopeful that therapy can provide a way to process his emotions more healthily and find a path forward without losing the memory of Mary. His primary goal is to reclaim some semblance of normalcy and continue honoring her memory while also embracing new experiences and future possibilities.
